Plácido, can I ask you something personal? I’m thinking about leaving my job.
Of course, Arjun. What’s happening?
I’ve been working seventy hours a week for two years. I think I’m starting to burn out. But if I quit, I lose a good salary.
I understand. When I was your age, I almost stayed in a job I hated. If I had stayed, I would never have started my own company.
So you think I should take a risk?
Not blindly. Weigh up the options first. Do you have a safety net? Six months of savings, for example?
About four months. And my manager has offered me a different role, with fewer hours.
Then talk to him before you decide. With hindsight, the people I see regret are the ones who left angry, not the ones who left prepared.

People sometimes ask me what the turning point of my career was, and the answer always surprises them. It was the day I was laid off. I was thirty-two, working at a bank in London, and I was devastated. But if I hadn't been laid off, I would never have started my own business. I'd probably still be sitting at a desk in that bank, or retired from it. So with hindsight, it was the best thing that ever happened to me. Do I have regrets? One. When my children were young, I worked far too much. If I had taken more time for them then, I think I'd be closer to them now. I stepped down last year, at seventy, and that's the advice I give every young manager.

Here's what I see again and again. People quit on a bad day. They're exhausted, they're burned out, and they walk into their manager's office and resign. And six months later they say: if I'd waited a little, if I'd had a plan, it would have been so different. So before you quit, ask yourself three questions. One: am I leaving something, or am I going to something? Two: do I have a safety net? Three: have I actually talked to my manager? You'd be surprised how many problems can be solved with one honest conversation. And one last thing. The research is very clear: people regret the risks they didn't take much more than the ones they did.

I was an engineer in the car industry for twenty-five years. Then, at fifty, I decided to quit and open a bakery. Everybody thought I was crazy. Was it a risk? Of course. But I weighed it up for two years, and I had a safety net: my savings and my wife's salary. Today I have a small bakery in Lyon, and I've never been happier. Would I do anything differently? Yes, one thing. If I had found a mentor before I started, someone with experience in the business, I wouldn't have made so many mistakes in the first year. I lost a lot of money that I didn't need to lose. So find a mentor. It's the cheapest insurance in the world.
